lectures.title: Leveraging Command Output: the Command Substitution `$(...)`

cues.en: In this lecture, we now want to have a look at another expansion, the so-called command substitution.
This allows us to execute a command and use the output as a replacement for our expansion.
For this, we can use command substitution.
So for that we write a dollar sign, then the round brackets and then our command that we would like
to execute.
So for example, this here would execute this command, then take the result of that and that would
be put into this position where our expansion has been written.
It's still best to have double quotes around it so that we can disable word splitting here.
Otherwise word splitting will still be applied.
This will then execute this inner command in a so-called sub shell environment.
We can imagine that our bash process is starting another process that is then executing that command
and this is then collecting the output and then we can use this output just as an example, The PWD
program, for example, prints my current working directory.
But one thing I could do, for example, would be my current working directory is directory is, and
then I could try to here, for example, execute this program.
I would then collect the output and the output would then end up at this position here.
And then we can see this is now my current working directory.
Of course here, probably variable substitution would be a little bit more performant because this is
an environment variable.
But of course we could also invoke a program here and collect the output of that.
When using command substitution, it's best to use double quotes around them.
Single quotes do not work with the command substitution.
Why should we use double quotes around?
Well, here I'm in my current working directory and this current working directory contains a white
space.
So we have again this word splitting problem.
So for example, if I would use this command substitution like this to refer to a file.
So for example here command substitution dot txt.
I could try to output this, but if I would now try to create this file, we will see that this one
doesn't work.
This is because here again word splitting is at play.
So if I just put this into an echo again, then we can see this is the first file we are trying to create
and this is the second file that we are trying to create because word splitting is being applied here.
So it's best to always use this command substitution within double quotes and then we can see our CS
txt file that now has been created here properly.
Sometimes this command substitution can be extremely useful, especially if we want to build nice echo
outputs for our program.
So for example here, if we want to calculate the size of our home directory, we can use the disk usage
program and we are only interested in the sum of our home directory.
And so we want to do this calculation, we want to sum it and we want to have it printed in a human
readable format.
So here we are using command substitution and here we are just having a single quoted string to say
that we are now printing the size of our home directory.
So here, for example, if I want to execute this, the size of my home directory is then single quotes
end and then my command substitution du disk usage minus H of my home directory.
And then we can see here this is now the disk usage of my home directory.
Or another way would for example, be here.
There are this many files in our current directory.
This is a little bit tricky here.
Again, I want to use a single quote that's just printed there and I've chosen a relatively difficult
way to represent that.
But here we can see single quoted area ends here.
Then a double quoted area begins.
There's only a single quote inside.
So this word is printed there without any quotes.
Then a single quote is printed.
And then we start yet another single quoted area for R for R and white space.
We end that single quoted area because our command substitution doesn't work within the single quoted
area.
Then we enter a double quoted area so that our command substitution works and then we leave that double
quoted area again and we enter a single quoted area again for the rest of that line.
Of course, maybe just putting double quotes around the whole sentence might have been a little bit
easier, but why do it easy?
If we can also do it in a more difficult way, then I can explain a little bit more here.
If we just want to see whether that command actually works, then I can just paste it here.
And we can see here right now there are 29 files in my current directory.
This is command substitution.
But there's also one more way to write it.
This is a little bit less common and we should not really use it that much because it's a bit more difficult
to see.
And here we can see that we are using the backticks.
These are not the normal single quotes.
Those are backticks.
There's it really depends on your local, on your keyboard layout, how to produce those.
But here we can see that this is also a command substitution because of those backticks.
This is considered to be less readable and I would not recommend using it here.
In my case I can do this.
Those backticks it's next to my backspace key.
And then after that I need to press a space to enable this backtick on the US keyboard.
That backtick key should usually be below the escape key.
So now I'm entering this command substitution area.
I will say that this is the command and then I use double quotes again to prevent any additional words
or any word splitting here.
And if we do this, we can see here this output of our program is now being outputted through Echo.
By the way, in case you are wondering, why is it newlines?
This is because our LHS detects whether it's printing directly to the terminal or whether the output
is being collected here.
In this case, the output is being collected not because we are in a pipe or we are in a redirect,
but it's being collected because we are within a command substitution.
This also counts as output collection and if that's the case, then LHS prints every element in a new
line.
So it's easier for our operators to work on those.
So this is why it's now printed here in different lines.
But aside from that, this is the normal LHS output now.
So this would now be here, this command substitution and how you can use this to execute commands and
use that result in your existing commands.
